sentences.text: OLMoTrace is a tracing tool in the census's lineage of training data, attaching provenance to "a span of a language model's output and the training documents that contain it verbatim" (provenance census record), and its authors present it as "the first system that traces the outputs of language models back to their full, multi-trillion-token training data in real time" (arXiv:2504.07096).

Ai2 introduced it on 9 April 2025 as a feature of the Ai2 Playground (Ai2 blog), and the census answers its organizing question for it, "What provenance does this system carry, through which operation, on whose assertion, with what evidence of survival?", field by field (census record).

The relation it carries is a verbatim match: it "finds and shows verbatim matches between segments of language model output and documents in the training text corpora" (arXiv abstract), highlighting long and unique spans found at least once in the training data (Ai2 blog), which the census records as its one relation type, its operation (model generation traced back to training text) and its unit, "a maximal matching span of model output" (census record).

It retrieves "by lexical overlap, with the heuristic that such training examples are likely to be influential for the given output" (the paper, §6); for the class of training-data attribution, which treats model behaviour as counterfactually dependent on the examples that entered training, the archive's protocol ranks exact paired retraining first, validated approximation second, and "unvalidated similarity or intuition only as exploratory evidence" (#1075).

Its carrier is the model's full training corpus over an extended infini-gram index (census record): for OLMo-2-32B-Instruct, 3.2 billion documents and 4.6 trillion tokens across pre-, mid- and post-training, all of them matched (the paper; Ai2 blog; census record).

Span finding runs at O(L * log N) (Ai2 blog); up to 10 enclosing snippets are retrieved per kept span and ranked by BM25 (the paper), a score that conveys "some notion of relevance" (Ai2 blog), behind a "Show OLMoTrace" button below the model's answer (Techzine, snippet only).

Per query the tracing takes 4.46 seconds on average, and the first document it displays averages 1.90 on a 0–3 relevance scale, roughly "on the same topic" as the output, in the paper's own measurement (the paper).

At launch it served OLMo 2 32B and 13B Instruct and OLMoE 1B 7B Instruct and "can be applied to any language model for which you have access to the training data" (Ai2 blog), "as long as the service provider has access to its full training data" (the paper); Ai2's post on X gives the OLMo 3 family (X, snippet only), which the Capture Registry finds the census record does not yet carry and is to carry from Ai2's own page (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

The census tags it as tracing "only models whose training data is open" (census record); Farhadi ties the connection to Ai2's open inputs, and Liu expects closed-model providers to hesitate because the tool would expose their training data (Ken Yeung).

Its purpose, in the paper, is to explore where models "may have learned to generate certain word sequences", verbatim matching taken as "the most direct connection between LM outputs and the training data" (the paper), for researchers, developers and the general public (Ai2 blog), at "an early stage" of exploring the tool (Ai2 blog).

The archive places the class this tool belongs to on the training/output relation: data attribution asks "Which training examples shaped a specific output", an adjacent method that "Operates on training/output relation; PER operates on output/reader relation" (#725).

Of that class the archive holds that partial tracing "is possible at cost", that it does not recover authorship, and that "what survives depends on what is recorded and computed" (#1714), and that training-data attribution is the post-hoc detection layer, developed "in isolation" from the other survival layers, no system bundling them (#127).

Claims drawn from a model's training-time parameters, on the archive's typology, often carry no surface signal of the sources that contributed; PER reaches them only indirectly, and the substrate level needs companion infrastructure, "training-data provenance records" among it (#95), since provenance "has to survive the training pipeline" (#1714).

Its authors show it on "fact checking, hallucination, and the creativity of language models" (arXiv abstract), with three case studies, fact checking first (the paper), and Ai2's post traces a math expression the model could have learned by memorization and a false knowledge cutoff to post-training examples, a finding that changed the 32B model's post-training data (Ai2 blog).

Fact checking stands in the paper as a possibility, users "may be able to fact-check the statement against its training data", with its qualification that context and source help "a more informed judgment on the factuality of the statement", since words mislead out of context and some web sources are unreliable (the paper, arXiv v2 and ACL 2025).

Ai2's post calls the interpretation of matches "quite nuanced" and makes confidence in a generated fact conditional on the user's own check that the documents "come from trusted sources" (Ai2 blog); the newsletter calls it an application "offering fact-checking", and Liu's launch statement says users "can ensure that the data supporting their outputs is trustworthy and verifiable" (Ken Yeung).

The authors state the limit in both versions of the paper, "The retrieved documents should not be interpreted as having a causal effect on the LM output, or as supporting evidence or citations for the LM output" (the paper; ACL 2025), and the census carries it as two negative tags, not causes of the output and "NOT a citation system", and in what it records as surviving (census record).
To the newsletter Ai2 called the documents associations, not "the definitive source of the model's learning", and its results not "indicators of authority" (Ken Yeung).

Ai2's leaders tie the tool to hallucination scores, "assuming that the inputs were factual" (Farhadi), and to regulation, governance and auditability (Lebrecht), in the newsletter's report (Ken Yeung).

The paper sets it apart from retrieval-augmented generation, naming Google AI Overview among RAG's examples: OLMoTrace "retrieves documents post-hoc and does not intervene with the LM generation" (the paper; Liu in Ken Yeung), and Gemini's double-check, drawn from Search and not from Gemini's training data, is "less useful for scientific exploration" (the paper).

At its own name on Google's AI Overview, 2026-10-29, the composition held the tool, its maker, its real time, its scale and its verbatim matching, checked against the census record and the pages it saved, naming the tool, its method, its models and its uses (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29), and gave as its first use "Fact-Checking: Verify whether specific claims in a model's answer are backed by real training documents", a verbatim match "offered as support for a claim, the reading the paper excludes" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

The registry reads this as "the conversion of a matching relation into a citation relation that the paper names and refuses", a tool whose authors state what a match does not mean "composed with that meaning restored", and it finds the census record's negative tags to be the authors' own (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

Its 31 authors are at the Allen Institute for AI, the University of Washington, UC Berkeley and Stanford (arXiv; the paper), the operator the census records whole (census record), where the composition named Ai2 alone (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

It is "publicly available and fully open-source" (arXiv abstract), its core under the Apache 2.0 license (the paper), reached through the Ai2 Playground (census record), an expression of Ai2's commitment to "open models, open data, and beyond" (Ai2 blog).

Submitted 9 April 2025 and revised 8 July (arXiv; census record), it appeared in ACL 2025's System Demonstrations with the Best Demo award (ACL Anthology), and the census records it active, "ACL 2025 demo track" (census record).

Its authors name as a risk that it makes problematic training content "more easily exposed" (the paper), and the newsletter finds that it gives no analytics for improving the data: "Simply put, it's generating awareness" (Ken Yeung).

The census records the tool as one that records provenance, a neighbour of the Data Provenance Initiative, with the Playground and "infini-gram as a separate record" left unchecked (census record); no card cites the record, which landed the same day (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29), and Wikipedia has no article on OLMoTrace (Wikipedia, 2026-10-29).

L_BA.text: OLMoTrace is a tracing tool in the census's lineage of training data, attaching provenance to "a span of a language model's output and the training documents that contain it verbatim" (provenance census record), and its authors present it as "the first system that traces the outputs of language models back to their full, multi-trillion-token training data in real time" (arXiv:2504.07096). Ai2 introduced it on 9 April 2025 as a feature of the Ai2 Playground (Ai2 blog), and the census answers its organizing question for it, "What provenance does this system carry, through which operation, on whose assertion, with what evidence of survival?", field by field (census record). The relation it carries is a verbatim match: it "finds and shows verbatim matches between segments of language model output and documents in the training text corpora" (arXiv abstract), highlighting long and unique spans found at least once in the training data (Ai2 blog), which the census records as its one relation type, its operation (model generation traced back to training text) and its unit, "a maximal matching span of model output" (census record). It retrieves "by lexical overlap, with the heuristic that such training examples are likely to be influential for the given output" (the paper, §6); for the class of training-data attribution, which treats model behaviour as counterfactually dependent on the examples that entered training, the archive's protocol ranks exact paired retraining first, validated approximation second, and "unvalidated similarity or intuition only as exploratory evidence" (#1075). Its carrier is the model's full training corpus over an extended infini-gram index (census record): for OLMo-2-32B-Instruct, 3.2 billion documents and 4.6 trillion tokens across pre-, mid- and post-training, all of them matched (the paper; Ai2 blog; census record). Span finding runs at O(L * log N) (Ai2 blog); up to 10 enclosing snippets are retrieved per kept span and ranked by BM25 (the paper), a score that conveys "some notion of relevance" (Ai2 blog), behind a "Show OLMoTrace" button below the model's answer (Techzine, snippet only). Per query the tracing takes 4.46 seconds on average, and the first document it displays averages 1.90 on a 0–3 relevance scale, roughly "on the same topic" as the output, in the paper's own measurement (the paper). At launch it served OLMo 2 32B and 13B Instruct and OLMoE 1B 7B Instruct and "can be applied to any language model for which you have access to the training data" (Ai2 blog), "as long as the service provider has access to its full training data" (the paper); Ai2's post on X gives the OLMo 3 family (X, snippet only), which the Capture Registry finds the census record does not yet carry and is to carry from Ai2's own page (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). The census tags it as tracing "only models whose training data is open" (census record); Farhadi ties the connection to Ai2's open inputs, and Liu expects closed-model providers to hesitate because the tool would expose their training data (Ken Yeung). Its purpose, in the paper, is to explore where models "may have learned to generate certain word sequences", verbatim matching taken as "the most direct connection between LM outputs and the training data" (the paper), for researchers, developers and the general public (Ai2 blog), at "an early stage" of exploring the tool (Ai2 blog). The archive places the class this tool belongs to on the training/output relation: data attribution asks "Which training examples shaped a specific output", an adjacent method that "Operates on training/output relation; PER operates on output/reader relation" (#725). Of that class the archive holds that partial tracing "is possible at cost", that it does not recover authorship, and that "what survives depends on what is recorded and computed" (#1714), and that training-data attribution is the post-hoc detection layer, developed "in isolation" from the other survival layers, no system bundling them (#127). Claims drawn from a model's training-time parameters, on the archive's typology, often carry no surface signal of the sources that contributed; PER reaches them only indirectly, and the substrate level needs companion infrastructure, "training-data provenance records" among it (#95), since provenance "has to survive the training pipeline" (#1714). Its authors show it on "fact checking, hallucination, and the creativity of language models" (arXiv abstract), with three case studies, fact checking first (the paper), and Ai2's post traces a math expression the model could have learned by memorization and a false knowledge cutoff to post-training examples, a finding that changed the 32B model's post-training data (Ai2 blog). Fact checking stands in the paper as a possibility, users "may be able to fact-check the statement against its training data", with its qualification that context and source help "a more informed judgment on the factuality of the statement", since words mislead out of context and some web sources are unreliable (the paper, arXiv v2 and ACL 2025). Ai2's post calls the interpretation of matches "quite nuanced" and makes confidence in a generated fact conditional on the user's own check that the documents "come from trusted sources" (Ai2 blog); the newsletter calls it an application "offering fact-checking", and Liu's launch statement says users "can ensure that the data supporting their outputs is trustworthy and verifiable" (Ken Yeung). The authors state the limit in both versions of the paper, "The retrieved documents should not be interpreted as having a causal effect on the LM output, or as supporting evidence or citations for the LM output" (the paper; ACL 2025), and the census carries it as two negative tags, not causes of the output and "NOT a citation system", and in what it records as surviving (census record). To the newsletter Ai2 called the documents associations, not "the definitive source of the model's learning", and its results not "indicators of authority" (Ken Yeung). Ai2's leaders tie the tool to hallucination scores, "assuming that the inputs were factual" (Farhadi), and to regulation, governance and auditability (Lebrecht), in the newsletter's report (Ken Yeung). The paper sets it apart from retrieval-augmented generation, naming Google AI Overview among RAG's examples: OLMoTrace "retrieves documents post-hoc and does not intervene with the LM generation" (the paper; Liu in Ken Yeung), and Gemini's double-check, drawn from Search and not from Gemini's training data, is "less useful for scientific exploration" (the paper). At its own name on Google's AI Overview, 2026-10-29, the composition held the tool, its maker, its real time, its scale and its verbatim matching, checked against the census record and the pages it saved, naming the tool, its method, its models and its uses (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29), and gave as its first use "Fact-Checking: Verify whether specific claims in a model's answer are backed by real training documents", a verbatim match "offered as support for a claim, the reading the paper excludes" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). The registry reads this as "the conversion of a matching relation into a citation relation that the paper names and refuses", a tool whose authors state what a match does not mean "composed with that meaning restored", and it finds the census record's negative tags to be the authors' own (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). Its 31 authors are at the Allen Institute for AI, the University of Washington, UC Berkeley and Stanford (arXiv; the paper), the operator the census records whole (census record), where the composition named Ai2 alone (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). It is "publicly available and fully open-source" (arXiv abstract), its core under the Apache 2.0 license (the paper), reached through the Ai2 Playground (census record), an expression of Ai2's commitment to "open models, open data, and beyond" (Ai2 blog). Submitted 9 April 2025 and revised 8 July (arXiv; census record), it appeared in ACL 2025's System Demonstrations with the Best Demo award (ACL Anthology), and the census records it active, "ACL 2025 demo track" (census record). Its authors name as a risk that it makes problematic training content "more easily exposed" (the paper), and the newsletter finds that it gives no analytics for improving the data: "Simply put, it's generating awareness" (Ken Yeung). The census records the tool as one that records provenance, a neighbour of the Data Provenance Initiative, with the Playground and "infini-gram as a separate record" left unchecked (census record); no card cites the record, which landed the same day (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29), and Wikipedia has no article on OLMoTrace (Wikipedia, 2026-10-29).

The provenance census record describes OLMoTrace from its authors' own pages, each field with its basis ('operator'), and answers for it the census's question of what provenance a system carries, through which operation, on whose assertion, with what evidence of survival; the capture record checks the composition against those pages (CAP-1-01–CAP-1-02). The deposits bear on its class, tracing model outputs to training data, and add senses and limits on the field's own object: the training/output relation against PER's output/reader relation (#725), partial tracing at cost that recovers no authorship (#1714), the post-hoc detection layer developed in isolation (#127), similarity as exploratory evidence only (#1075), and the parametric claims such records are companion infrastructure for (#95). #725 states its own relation to the frameworks it places in these terms ('Extension and completion, not substitution or critique'). No defining paper contests the field's ontology of the tool or supplies one the field lacks: ρ = extends, the equal-terms case (§0.9, §1.2a). loci.quote: **Relation:** Extension and completion, not substitution or critique

| Data attribution (TRAK, influence functions) | Which training examples shaped a specific output | Adjacent eval method | Operates on training/output relation; PER operates on output/reader relation |

The attribution literature shows that partial tracing is possible at cost: influence-function methods estimate which training examples most affect a given output (Grosse et al. 2023). Neither recovers authorship, and both show that what survives depends on what is recorded and computed.

Parametric claims are drawn from the model's training-time parameters rather than runtime retrieval, often without surface signal indicating which sources materially contributed; PER applies to these only indirectly, and addressing them at the substrate level requires companion infrastructure (training-data provenance records, watermarking, content credentials).
What provenance does this system carry, through which operation, on whose assertion, with what evidence of survival?
a span of a language model's output and the training documents that contain it verbatim
The composition turns a trace of verbatim overlap into evidence for a claim, the conversion of a matching relation into a citation relation that the paper names and refuses.
